Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA .

Large pretrained models have achieved strong performance across a wide range of downstream tasks, alongside scaling parameters and training corpus ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2021 ) . Efficient generation has also been explored through leap multi-token prediction ( Liu et al., 2025b ) . In deployment, however, full-parameter fine-tuning for particular tasks or domains typically necessitates updating and storing full set of weights, motivating parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ; He et al., 2021 ) . By optimizing only a small set of task-specific parameters, it significantly reduces the adaptation cost. Among PEFT methods, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become a widely used and effective choice, learning compact task-specific updates that can be merged into pretrained weights for inference ( Hu et al., 2021 ) .

The principle behind LoRA is to leverage low-rank trainable factors to approximate dense weight updates ( Aghajanyan et al., 2021 ; Hu et al., 2021 ) . Specifically, for a pretrained weight 𝑾 0 {\bm{W}}_{0} , LoRA parameterizes the task-specific update as Δ ​ 𝑾 = 𝑩 ​ 𝑨 \Delta{\bm{W}}={\bm{B}}{\bm{A}} , which satisfies r = rank ​ ( 𝑩 ​ 𝑨 ) ≪ d r=\text{rank}({\bm{B}}{\bm{A}})\ll d , where d d denotes the dimension of 𝑾 {\bm{W}} . 𝑾 0 {\bm{W}}_{0} remains frozen during the fine-tuning phase. Therefore, it substantially reduces the number of trainable parameters, and the learned update can be merged into W 0 W_{0} without additional inference overhead. This balance of parameter efficiency and effective task specialization has kept LoRA widely used in resource-constrained settings. Recent advances continue to refine its low-rank principle through adaptive rank allocation ( Zhang et al., 2023b ) , initialization informed by pretrained weights or task gradients ( Meng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , optimization strategies tailored to its factorized parameterization ( Hayou et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) and adaptive adapter selection and placement ( Hayou et al., 2026 ; Veprikov et al., 2026 ) . Despite different methods to improve LoRA, they leave a fundamental question unanswered: does the learned update make effective use of its allocated rank?

To this end, we train a LoRA model with rank r = 16 r=16 for diagnosis and decompose each learned update Δ ​ 𝑾 \Delta{\bm{W}} using singular value decomposition (SVD). Without retraining, we evaluate rank- k k approximations formed by retaining the top k k singular components. As shown in Figure 1 , we find that k = 3 k=3 yields the best downstream performance, whereas retaining additional components degrades it. This suggests that the full learned update is less effective than a lower-rank approximation of itself. A larger rank budget does not necessarily produce a more useful task-specific update. Figure 1: Effect of retained rank on accuracy. Model performance does not improve monotonically with increasing retained rank.

Motivated by this observation, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation ( ReGRA ), which helps the learned LoRA update make more effective use of its available rank. ReGRA first trains a standard LoRA adapter and then estimates task gradients with a small subset of the training data. To exhaust the allocated rank, we initialize a second-stage adapter with task gradients projected onto the two-sided complement of the first-stage update. With this first-stage estimation, we are able to leave the previously learned components unchanged, yet continually fulfil the update within the allocated rank. During second-stage training, we apply orthogonal regularization to maintain decorrelation between the two stages. After training, both updates can be merged into the base model, introducing no additional inference cost. We evaluate ReGRA using standard LoRA evaluation following ( Hu et al., 2023 ) and expand it to natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. Under the same total-rank budget, ReGRA consistently achieves stronger overall performance across the evaluated benchmarks and even reaches the performance of the double-rank model. Ablation studies and further analysis support the effectiveness of residual-gradient initialization and update decorrelation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We reveal that standard LoRA training does not always make effective use of its allocated rank. We approach this problem from a task-gradient perspective, targeting directions not captured by the initial update.

• We propose ReGRA to exhaust the allocated rank. ReGRA is a two-stage adaptation method that estimates task gradients after standard LoRA training, projects out the components captured by the first-stage update, and uses the residual gradients to initialize a second-stage adapter. An orthogonal regularization maintains the decorrelation between the two updates. • We evaluate ReGRA on diverse benchmark sets, showing that it outperforms representative baselines and, in some settings, matches the performance of a model with twice the rank. Ablation studies support the efficacy and rationale of our design.

Low-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) represents task-specific weight updates using two trainable low-rank factors, reducing the number of trainable parameters while retaining mergeability at inference ( Hu et al., 2021 ) . Subsequent variants improve its memory and parameter efficiency through quantization, factor freezing, or shared random projections ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2023a ; Kopiczko et al., 2024 ) . Other methods explore adaptive rank allocation and rank-dependent scaling ( Zhang et al., 2023b ; Valipour et al., 2023 ; Kalajdzievski, 2023 ) . LoRA+, DoRA, and LoRA-Pro instead improve the optimization or parameterization of low-rank updates ( Hayou et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . Recent works also explore adaptive adapter selection and placement to determine where low-rank adaptation is most effective ( Hayou et al., 2026 ; Veprikov et al., 2026 ) . Although these methods improve LoRA from different perspectives, they do not explicitly investigate redundancy among rank components within a learned update matrix.

Spectral and gradient-informed initialization. Several methods initialize LoRA using information from pretrained weights, activations, or downstream data. PiSSA initializes adapters from the principal singular components of pretrained weights, whereas MiLoRA adapts their minor singular components ( Meng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . CorDA constructs context-aware adaptation subspaces from weight and activation statistics, while EVA selects initialization directions according to activation variance ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Paischer et al., 2026 ) . Gradient-based methods use the task gradient at the start of fine-tuning to guide adapter initialization ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Ponkshe et al., 2024 ) . These approaches determine the adaptation subspace before fine-tuning, whereas ReGRA estimates residual task gradients after a first-stage update has been learned.

Sequential and subspace-aware adaptation. ReLoRA and Chain of LoRA (COLA) construct higher-rank effective updates by repeatedly training, merging, and reinitializing low-rank adapters ( Lialin et al., 2024 ; Xia et al., 2024 ) . LoRA-based adaptation has also been studied in continual learning. CoLoR applies LoRA to domain-incremental learning ( Wistuba et al., 2023 ) , while O-LoRA assigns sequential tasks to orthogonal low-rank subspaces and InfLoRA constructs adaptation subspaces that reduce interference with prior tasks ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Liang and Li, 2024 ) . KeepLoRA further uses residual-gradient information to balance knowledge retention and plasticity across tasks ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . CMCL uses dual-sided gradient projection to reduce forgetting in continual learning ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . Unlike these methods, ReGRA considers two-stage adaptation to the same downstream objective and combines residual-gradient initialization with update decorrelation to encourage complementary stage-wise updates. Figure 2: Overall framework of Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA). ReGRA first trains Adapter 1 to learn an initial task-specific update. It then projects the task gradient away from the subspace already captured by Adapter 1 and extracts the dominant residual directions via SVD. These residual directions are used to initialize and guide Adapter 2 toward complementary task-relevant information. The two adapters are finally combined with the frozen backbone to form the final model.

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The pretrained weight 𝑾 0 {\bm{W}}_{0} remains frozen during adaptation. Several extensions modify how LoRA updates are trained or initialized. QLoRA reduces memory use by quantizing the frozen backbone ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) , while AdaLoRA and DyLoRA explore flexible rank allocation ( Zhang et al., 2023b ; Valipour et al., 2023 ) . LoRA-GA uses the initial task gradient to guide adapter initialization ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . The matrices 𝑼 ∈ ℝ d out × k {\bm{U}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times k} and 𝑽 ∈ ℝ d in × k {\bm{V}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times k} contain the left and right singular vectors, respectively, while 𝚺 = diag ⁡ ( σ 1 , … , σ k ) {\bm{\Sigma}}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k}) contains the positive singular values in descending order. The columns of 𝑼 {\bm{U}} span the output-side directions represented by the update, whereas the columns of 𝑽 {\bm{V}} span its input-side directions. These singular subspaces are used to identify which components of a task gradient are already represented by a learned low-rank update. Spectral information has also been used to initialize LoRA adapters: PiSSA selects the principal singular components of the pretrained weights ( Meng et al., 2024 ) , while MiLoRA selects the minor components ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . Here, we apply SVD to the first-stage update Δ ​ 𝑾 \Delta{\bm{W}} to identify the components of the task gradient already captured by the update.

Computation and inference. Residual-gradient calibration introduces a one-time cost between the two training stages. Each dense task gradient is formed only transiently, projected, compressed to rank q q , and then discarded, while cross-batch aggregation and update decorrelation operate on low-rank factors. After training, the two learned updates are merged into the pretrained weight as 𝑾 merged = 𝑾 0 + s 1 ​ 𝑩 1 ​ 𝑨 1 + s 2 ​ 𝑩 2 ​ 𝑨 2 {\bm{W}}_{\mathrm{merged}}={\bm{W}}_{0}+s_{1}{\bm{B}}_{1}{\bm{A}}_{1}+s_{2}{\bm{B}}_{2}{\bm{A}}_{2} . The Stage-2 procedure is detailed in Appendix B.4 . ReGRA therefore introduces neither an additional adapter branch nor extra computation during inference, storage and computation bounds are given in Appendix B.6 .

To validate the efficacy and rationale of our design, we conduct experiments to address the following research questions (RQs): • RQ1: How does ReGRA compare with baselines across diverse benchmark sets, and how does it compare with LoRA with larger rank capacity ( i.e. , r = 8 r=8 v.s. r = 16 r=16 )? • RQ2: What are the separate and combined effects of residual-gradient initialization and update decorrelation? • RQ3: Which singular components of a trained LoRA update affect performance when removed, and what do isolated components of ReGRA’s second-stage update contribute? • RQ4: How does performance change as rank-2 stages are progressively added?

Tasks and datasets. We evaluate ReGRA on natural language understanding ( Wang et al., 2018 ) , mathematical reasoning ( Hu et al., 2023 ; Cobbe et al., 2021 ) ,and code generation ( Chen et al., 2021 ; Austin et al., 2021 ) . For natural language understanding, we fine-tune RoBERTa-base and RoBERTa-large ( Liu et al., 2019 ) separately on the eight GLUE tasks: CoLA, SST-2, MRPC, STS-B, QQP, MNLI, QNLI, and RTE. We evaluate all tasks on their labeled validation sets, with the matched validation split used for MNLI. For mathematical reasoning ( Hu et al., 2023 ) , we fine-tune Llama-3-8B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and Qwen3-8B-Base ( Yang et al., 2025 ) on Math-7K training set released with LLM-Adapters ( Hu et al., 2023 ) . We evaluate on AddSub, MultiArith, SingleEq, GSM8K, AQuA, and SVAMP. For code generation, we fine-tune Llama-3-8B on CodeFeedback-Filtered-Instruction ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) and evaluate on MBPP ( Austin et al., 2021 ) and its enhanced MBPP+ test suite using EvalPlus ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . Implementation details. Adapters are applied to the query, key, and value projections while the pretrained backbones remain frozen, details are provided in Appendix B.1 . Each ReGRA stage uses rank 8, α = 16 \alpha=16 , and dropout 0.05; the GLUE classification head is trained in the first stage and frozen in the second stage. Generative losses are computed only on response tokens. We use zero weight decay, and λ t = 0.1 \lambda_{\mathrm{t}}=0.1 , whose contribution is warmed up over the first 100 second-stage steps. The training schedules for GLUE, mathematics, and code generation comprise 20, 2, and 1 epochs, respectively, full settings are tabulated in Appendix B.3 .

Baselines and evaluation. We compare ReGRA with LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) , DoRA ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , PiSSA ( Meng et al., 2024 ) , LoRA-One ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and KeepLoRA ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . LoRA is evaluated at ranks 8 and 16, while the other baselines use rank 8. For ReGRA, r = 8 r=8 refers to the rank of each stage. GLUE uses the standard task-specific metrics: Matthews correlation for CoLA, the mean of Pearson and Spearman correlations for STS-B, the mean of accuracy and F 1 F_{1} for MRPC and QQP, and accuracy otherwise. Mathematical reasoning uses answer accuracy, and code generation uses pass@1. All scores are reported as percentages.

As shown in Table 1 , ReGRA achieves the highest average score on both backbones. Increasing the rank of standard LoRA from 8 to 16 also improves its average score, confirming that additional low-rank capacity is useful. ReGRA obtains a further improvement at the same maximum update rank by guiding how that capacity is used. After learning the first-stage update, ReGRA initializes the second adapter from task-gradient directions outside the subspace associated with that update. Update-level decorrelation then discourages the two stage-wise updates from aligning during training. Standard rank-16 LoRA optimizes all rank components jointly without this explicit guidance toward complementary updates. The comparison supports the benefit of directing added capacity toward optimization directions left insufficiently covered by the first stage. Gains on CoLA, MRPC, and RTE further support this pattern.

Table 2 shows that ReGRA achieves the highest six-task average on both Llama-3-8B and Qwen3-8B-Base. The task-level pattern differs between the backbones. On Llama-3-8B, the gains over rank-8 LoRA are concentrated on AddSub, SVAMP, and AQuA, while MultiArith declines. Its average also exceeds rank-16 LoRA on both backbones, though the margin is small on Qwen3-8B-Base. These results show that the overall mathematical-reasoning benefit carries across two generative backbones, with different task-level patterns. Code generation (RQ1). To disentangle the effects of the two key design components of ReGRA, we conduct a controlled 2 × 2 2\times 2 ablation study on the mathematical reasoning benchmarks. All variants share the same rank-8 first-stage adapter and train an additional rank-8 Stage-2 adapter under identical optimization settings. When residual-gradient initialization is removed, the second-stage adapter adopts the standard LoRA initialization, with a randomly initialized input-side factor and a zero-initialized output-side factor. When update-level decorrelation is removed, the corresponding regularization term is omitted from the Stage-2 objective. Performance is measured by the unweighted average accuracy across the six mathematical reasoning datasets. As shown in Figure 4 , residual-gradient initialization provides the dominant improvement, supporting the motivation of directing second-stage adaptation toward gradient information insufficiently captured by the first-stage. Update-level decorrelation provides a smaller additional benefit by discouraging redundancy between the two updates. The full model achieves the strongest overall performance, suggesting that the two components play complementary roles: the former determines informative adaptation directions, while the latter encourages the resulting update to remain distinct from the first-stage.

We further examine how individual directions in a trained rank-16 LoRA update affect downstream performance. We decompose each learned update using SVD, remove one singular component at a time, and evaluate the resulting model. As shown in Figure 5 , removing the leading singular component produces the largest performance drop in all three evaluations: 3.97 percentage points on both MBPP and MBPP+, and 8.03 percentage points on Math. Removing most of the remaining components has a much smaller effect, and removing some even improves performance slightly. These leave-one-component-out results measure the functional effect of each removal, beyond the magnitude of its singular value. Together with the top- k k analysis in Figure 1 , they indicate that the learned LoRA directions do not contribute uniformly to task performance. This observation motivates ReGRA to seek complementary directions from the residual gradient after the first-stage update has been learned.

To examine the functional contribution of the learned Stage-2 update, we decompose each trained Stage-2 update matrix by SVD and evaluate eight independent variants. Variant C i C_{i} retains only the i i th rank-one component in each adapted matrix while keeping Stage 1 fixed; the variants are not cumulative. As shown in Figure 6 , their effects differ across task families. On the six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, only C 3 C_{3} , C 4 C_{4} , and C 6 C_{6} improve mean accuracy over Stage 1-only, by 2.91, 1.27, and 0.56 percentage points, respectively; the other five components produce small decreases. The full Stage-2 update gains 1.27 points, below C 3 C_{3} alone. On MBPP+, seven components improve pass@1 by 0.79–1.85 points, while C 6 C_{6} leaves it unchanged; the full update gains 2.65 points. These results show heterogeneous and task-dependent component effects. The full update’s benchmark performance is not a sum of its isolated component effects, although these independent evaluations do not identify each component’s marginal contribution within the full update, example-level error analyses are reported in Appendix C.2 .

Figure 7: Progressive rank expansion on LLaMA-3-8B. At each stage, previously learned adapters are frozen and a new rank-2 adapter is trained. Progressive Rank Expansion (RQ4). We further evaluate our method on LLaMA-3-8B under a multi-stage training setting. Starting from the base model, we iteratively train a new rank-2 adapter at each stage while freezing all previously learned adapters. Therefore, the effective adaptation rank increases progressively as more adapters are accumulated. As shown in Fig. 7 , the overall performance consistently improves with the increasing cumulative rank, rising from 69.20% at rank 2 to 71.81% at rank 16. Although minor fluctuations are observed at intermediate ranks, the overall trend demonstrates that newly introduced adapters continue to provide complementary adaptation capacity rather than merely duplicating previously learned directions. These results support the effectiveness of our additive multi-stage training strategy for progressively expanding the model’s adaptation capacity.

In this work, we introduced ReGRA, a two-stage adaptation method that makes more effective use of a fixed total-rank budget. Motivated by the observation that additional LoRA singular components do not always improve performance, ReGRA uses residual task gradients to initialize a second adapter while preserving the first-stage solution. An orthogonality regularizer helps maintain separation between the two updates, which can be merged without additional inference overhead. Experiments on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation demonstrate improvements over rank-matched LoRA, while ablations support both design choices. These findings suggest that effective low-rank adaptation depends not only on increasing rank, but also on learning useful additional components relative to an existing update. Future work may investigate more principled ways to identify and allocate useful residual directions under a fixed rank budget.

This section specifies the model setup, residual-gradient calibration, training hyperparameters, algorithm flow, and computational cost of ReGRA.

We apply LoRA adapters to the query, key, and value projections. The pretrained backbone remains fixed during both training stages. Each ReGRA stage uses rank 8 8 , LoRA scaling parameter α = 16 \alpha=16 , and dropout 0.05 0.05 . Stage 1 trains a standard LoRA adapter on the task training data. Its learned update is then fixed during calibration and Stage-2 training. For GLUE, the task-specific classification head is trained in Stage 1 and retained without further updates in Stage 2. For generative tasks, the language-modeling loss is computed only on response tokens. Experiments use seed 42 42 , bfloat16 precision, and zero weight decay. The training runs were conducted on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090.

Calibration is performed once after Stage 1 and before Stage 2. We load the pretrained backbone together with the fixed Stage-1 adapter and evaluate task gradients on batches drawn from the training data. The selected calibration records are processed without data-loader shuffling. For each adapted weight, a gradient with respect to the underlying weight is computed without applying an optimizer update. Each gradient is projected using the first-stage left and right subspaces, as described in Appendix A.1 . The residual is immediately compressed to rank at most q q , and the dense gradient is discarded. Batchwise low-rank factors are aggregated using the procedure in Appendix A.2 . The leading right singular vectors of the aggregate initialize 𝑨 2 {\bm{A}}_{2} , while 𝑩 2 {\bm{B}}_{2} is initialized to zero. Consequently, the initialized Stage-2 adapter does not change the function represented by the Stage-1 model. For commonsense reasoning, the calibration subset contains 64 64 examples, with eight selected from each of the eight tasks. This task balancing applies only to calibration; it does not change the order of subsequent Stage-2 training.
